text.text: The practice in one place: clients, proposals with weighted value, engagements with days sold against days used, deliverables waiting on review, and the timesheet that feeds it all. Start on the Dashboard each Monday, then work Mine and the Overdue views.
Proposals out for decision, with value, chance and decision date.
Work in delivery, with days sold against days used.
The documents and workshops promised in each engagement.
Consultant days logged against each engagement.

This workspace runs a consulting practice: the clients and sponsors you work with, every proposal and its chance of winning, each engagement with the days sold against the days used, the deliverables you promised, and the timesheets behind them. Decks and models stay in your document tools; this is where the practice sees pipeline, delivery and margin together.

Look at the weighted value against the days your team has free over the next quarter. A thin pipeline needs business development now; a crowded one needs a hiring or scheduling decision.

pages.title: Days sold, days used and margin

text.text: Consulting margin is won or lost in days. Every engagement is sold as a number of days, and every extra day is paid for by the practice unless it is agreed.
Consultants log days weekly, in half days at least, against the engagement.

Write them short: what is added, how many days, the price, and the new end date. Signed before the work starts. A change order is a normal business conversation, not a failure.
Across the practice, look each month at billable days against available days for each consultant. Very high utilization for months burns people out; low utilization means the pipeline needs work.

The returns process review is in final readout with burn ahead of plan because the root-cause interviews took longer than planned. The deck is still drafting, so the lead limits the remaining work to the readout and logs the lesson for the next proposal.
After each engagement closes, compare days sold with days used by phase. Use the real numbers to price the next similar proposal.
The final readout is where the client decides what the work was worth, and often whether there will be a next engagement. Prepare it like the most important meeting of the engagement, because it is.
